newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Credit Lyonnais shares suddenly in vogue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Credit Lyonnais shares suddenly in vogue.

text.p: Could shares in the French state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais, whose lending excesses in the 1980s brought it to the brink of bankruptcy, now be a buy?

Some investors think so which explains why the non voting publicly-held shares in the bank -- poised to get its third state aid package in four years -- have surged more than 140 percent since hitting a low of 94.55 francs ($16.53) in June.
The investment certificates, which represent 19 percent of the bank's capital, added another 3.54 percent on Friday, trading at 234.0 francs.

That is just over a quarter of the 900 franc peak they hit in May 1990 before a collapse in the French property market and a deep recession triggered the bad debt problems that almost brought about the bank's downfall.

Credit Lyonnais racked up losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 as a result of a wild expansion binge aimed at putting French banking on the world map. It limped back into profit in 1995 with a profit of 13 million francs.

Banking analysts emphasize the stock remains a speculative play and say its ultimate value will be dictated by the government's plan to ready the bank for privatisation that it will present to the European Union for approval in late March.
The government intends to sell the bank, once France's flagship financial institution, in early 1999.

"Credit Lyonnais' valuation at this juncture is largely in the hands of the French government, under the watchful eyes of the European Union..." said U.S. investment house Salomon Brothers which has a "hold" recommendation on the shares.
"We continue to view the valuation of Credit Lyonnais shares as more of a political call than a banking analysis," it said in a recent report.

Still, a number of investment houses have turned more positive on the stock recently in the belief that the bank's recovery strategy of refocusing on its commercial banking network at home and concentrating on wholesale banking abroad will pay off.

"Credit Lyonnais is currently the (French) bank the most undervalued by the market...with regard to a valuation that will be retained in a privatisation," said analyst Sami Gotrane of Paris brokerage EIFB, who has put the shares on "overweight".
FORECASTS FOR THE FUTURE

Didier Le Menestrel, who runs the Paris investment house Financiere de L'Echiquier, says Credit Lyonnais, known as the bank that couldn't say 'no' in its lending heyday, could outshine its rivals in years to come.

"My strong feeling is the profitability of Credit Lyonnais will be much greater in the years to come than its fellow (French) banks," he said. "Now its balance sheet has been cleaned up, it is a very clean bank."

Under a 1995 state bailout valued at 145 billion francs, the bank's dud assets acquired during the expansion spree that briefly made it the largest bank outside Japan were spun off into a state-owned shell company.

Le Menestrel said "coming close to death" had forced the bank to be more aggressive commercially and shake off the traditional French view of banking as a public service rather than as a business designed to generate profits.
Underpinning the new enthusiasm about Credit Lyonnais is a more positive feeling about French commercial banks as a whole amid signs of a long-awaited restructuring of the sector.
But analysts say the share is only for investors who don't mind risk and definitely not for "widow and orphan" portfolios.

"People are betting the taxpayer is going to pay for its troubles," said a Paris analyst. "Certainly the share may be undervalued -- but it reflects the fact there's no visibility on it. We don't know yet what the terms of the recapitalisation will be. There's no clean valuation."
"Even after it has got its act together, I'm not suggesting this will be a highly profitable bank," added a London analyst who has a 12-month price target of 230 francs.
SHARE VALUE DEPENDS ON BANK SELL-OFF
In determining the share's value, analysts say a huge amount hinges on the government's plan for selling the bank.

Analysts expect it to involve a state capital injection of 10 and 15 billion francs to boost the bank's solvency ratios to attract a buyer and cover losses on asset sales demanded by the European Commission in exchange for approving new state aid.

The Commission, responsible for ensuring state aid does not distort competition, is expected to insist Credit Lyonnais sell all its remaining European banking network outside France. It could impose additional penalties but France will argue that overly tough conditions might require even greater state aid.
Many of the bank's assets were bought at the market's peak and their sale is expected to trigger large capital losses.

Analysts believe the capital injection will most likely involve a shares-for-cash exchange that would mean a stock dilution. "The number of shares ultimately created in this process will be the key determinant of the value of the existing shares," said Salomon Brothers.
Its recapitalisation scenarios suggest a share price "perhaps centred in the 200-250 franc range".
Paris brokerage Dupont Denant estimated the recapitalisation would be 15 billion francs, meaning the creation of 79 million shares, and said the stock could be worth around 250 francs.
Gotrane, who believes the capital injection could be around 12 billion francs, said on that basis, the share "has a minimum value of 280 to 285 francs...but it could go to 300 or 310".
The bank's shares got a boost last month from a newspaper report saying it was poised for a big profit recovery this year.
Les Echos said the bank expected 1997 profits of 3.4 to 3.7 billion francs but that forecast mystified even the most positive analysts who expect profits of around 1.5 billion.
After last year's 13 million francs, analysts expect the bank to post a profit of around 150 million francs this year.
All this bullish sentiment, though, could backfire on Credit Lyonnais as the better its prospects, the tougher the conditions the European Commission could impose on it.

Its rivals could also be much louder in opposing the state help. Marc Vienot, chairman of private sector competitor Societe Generale, has already demanded the "controlled liquidation" of Credit Lyonnais.

Vienot said it would be "stunning if our fellow bank kept its profitable assets to compete with us and made the taxpayer foot the bill for the sale of its unprofitable assets". ($ = 5.718 French Francs)
